Reference: Butts (2023)

Model Setting

The paper formalizes the ring method, a widely used estimator for the effect of a spatially targeted treatment (a foreclosed home, a toxic plant, a new transit stop) observed with geocoded microdata. The method compares the change in outcomes of units immediately next to the treatment location, inside an inner ring, with the change for units slightly further away, inside an outer ring; all remaining units are dropped. The paper asks which assumptions make this comparison an unbiased estimate of the average treatment effect on the affected units, what the estimator returns when they fail, and how to do better. Two assumptions are needed. The first is parallel trends between the two rings, which applied work motivates by saying that units in a small neighborhood share the same shocks. The second is that the researcher knows exactly how far treatment effects reach, so that the inner ring contains all affected units and only those. If the inner ring is too narrow, affected units contaminate the control ring; if it is too wide, unaffected units are averaged into the treated ring and the estimate is attenuated towards zero.

The proposed alternative uses the stronger form of the first assumption (a counterfactual trend that is constant across distance within the outer ring) to drop the second. A partitioning-based least squares estimator (binscatter) in the sense of Cattaneo, Farrell and Feng and of Cattaneo, Crump, Farrell and Feng splits the sample into many quantile-spaced rings, with the number of rings chosen by the data, and estimates a treatment effect curve as the difference between each ring's mean change and the mean change of the outermost ring. It only requires that effects die out somewhere inside the outer ring, not that the researcher knows where. The plotted curve also serves as an informal check of the trend assumption, in the spirit of a pre-trends test in an event study. Re-analysing Linden and Rockoff (2008) on the arrival of a registered sex offender, the paper finds that the published single-ring estimate (a decline in home prices of about 7.5 percent within one tenth of a mile) hides a decline of around 20 percent in the two closest rings and no significant effect in the rest of the original treated ring.

A Simulated Example

The motivating example is a city that cleans an overgrown empty lot, with a positive effect on nearby home prices that declines with distance and drops to zero at 0.75 miles, and a constant counterfactual trend normalized to zero. With the treated ring ending exactly at 0.75 miles and the control ring at 1.5 miles the ring estimate is 0.73. This single number hides large heterogeneity: some units have effects as small as half and others as large as twice that value. If the treated ring is too wide (1 mile), unaffected units enter the treated average and the estimate falls to 0.54. If it is too narrow (0.5 miles), affected units enter the control ring, which biases the estimated counterfactual trend upward, but the treated ring now holds only the closest units with the largest effects, and the estimate rises to 0.81. A fourth panel, with a treated ring of 0.25 miles and a control ring of 1 mile, also gives 0.81. A researcher who used it as a robustness check of the too-narrow specification would be reassured although both estimates are too large, so varying the rings is not a reliable check.

Identifying Assumptions

The central claim of applied work is that counterfactual trends evolve smoothly over distance, so that λ(Disti)\lambda(\text{Dist}_i)λ(Disti​) is approximately constant close to treatment. Assumption 2 (Local Parallel Trends) holds for a distance dˉ\bar{d}dˉ if:

λ(d)=λ(d′)for all positive d,d′≤dˉ(7)\lambda(d)=\lambda(d')\quad\text{for all positive }d,d'\leq\bar{d} \tag{7}λ(d)=λ(d′)for all positive d,d′≤dˉ(7)

In the absence of treatment, outcomes would evolve in the same way at every distance up to dˉ\bar{d}dˉ. It fails if the treatment location is targeted on trends within a small area, so that trends are not constant within the control ring, or if units sort towards or away from treatment in a way that is correlated with the outcome, so that composition changes over time. Local Parallel Trends implies the standard and weaker Assumption 3 (Average Parallel Trends), which holds for a pair of distances dtd_tdt​ and dcd_cdc​ if:

E[λ(Disti)∣0≤Disti≤dt]=E[λ(Disti)∣dt<Disti≤dc](8)\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(\text{Dist}_i)\mid0\leq\text{Dist}_i\leq d_t\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(\text{Dist}_i)\mid d_t<\text{Dist}_i\leq d_c\right] \tag{8}E[λ(Disti​)∣0≤Disti​≤dt​]=E[λ(Disti​)∣dt​<Disti​≤dc​](8)

(the paper writes λd\lambda_dλd​ and conditions on ddd). If Local Parallel Trends holds for some dcd_cdc​, then on the subsample D≡{i:Disti≤dc}\mathcal{D}\equiv\{i:\text{Dist}_i\leq d_c\}D≡{i:Disti​≤dc​} the first-difference equation becomes:

ΔYit=τ(Disti)+λ+Δεit(9)\Delta Y_{it}=\tau(\text{Dist}_i)+\lambda+\Delta\varepsilon_{it} \tag{9}ΔYit​=τ(Disti​)+λ+Δεit​(9)

where λ\lambdaλ is a constant. The treatment effect curve is therefore identified up to a constant under Assumption 2 alone. To pin down the constant, researchers claim that effects stop before some distance dt<dcd_t<d_cdt​<dc​. Assumption 4 (Correct dtd_tdt​) holds for a distance dtd_tdt​ if:

(i) τ(d)>0 for all d≤dt and τ(d)=0 for all d>dt;(ii) F(dc)−F(dt)>0(10)\text{(i) }\tau(d)>0\text{ for all }d\leq d_t\text{ and }\tau(d)=0\text{ for all }d>d_t;\qquad\text{(ii) }F(d_c)-F(d_t)>0 \tag{10}(i) τ(d)>0 for all d≤dt​ and τ(d)=0 for all d>dt​;(ii) F(dc​)−F(dt​)>0(10)

Proposition 1 (Decomposition of Ring Estimate) gives its expectation when units follow the model above. Part (i), with no further assumption:

The proof substitutes the first-difference equation into the two conditional means. This produces three differences between the rings: in τ(Disti)\tau(\text{Dist}_i)τ(Disti​), in λ(Disti)\lambda(\text{Dist}_i)λ(Disti​) and in Δεi\Delta\varepsilon_iΔεi​. The last is zero because the error is uncorrelated with distance by construction, which gives (i). Under either parallel trends assumption the trend difference is zero, which gives (ii). Under Assumption 4 the control ring contains no affected unit, so E[τ(Disti)∣Dc]=0\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist}_i)\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right]=0E[τ(Disti​)∣Dc​]=0, and the treated ring contains exactly the affected units, so its mean effect is τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ, which gives (iii).

The proposition shows what the ring estimator delivers in each case.

  • Trends differ: the second term of part (i) is a bias. Since treatment can be targeted, the treated ring may be on a different trend than units further away, and control units are then not a good counterfactual.

  • dtd_tdt​ too narrow: Dc\mathcal{D}_cDc​ contains units that experience treatment effects, and the average of these effects is subtracted from the estimate. Without knowledge of the curve τ(Dist)\tau(\text{Dist})τ(Dist) it is unclear whether β^1\hat{\beta}_1β^​1​ grows or shrinks, because the treated ring at the same time keeps only the closest units, but in general β^1\hat{\beta}_1β^​1​ is not unbiased for τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ.

  • dtd_tdt​ too wide: Dt\mathcal{D}_tDt​ contains units that are not affected, and β^1\hat{\beta}_1β^​1​ is biased towards zero.

  • dtd_tdt​ exactly right: β^1\hat{\beta}_1β^​1​ is unbiased for τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ, but it is one number that averages over the whole curve.

The attenuation in the too-wide case can be made explicit; the following line is implied by part (ii) and is not printed in the paper. Let d∗d^{*}d∗ (notation of this note) be the distance that satisfies Assumption 4 and suppose d∗<dtd^{*}<d_td∗<dt​. Then the control ring has zero effects, the treated ring mixes affected units with zeros, and:

E[β^1]=F(d∗)F(dt)τˉ(16)\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\beta}_1\right]=\frac{F(d^{*})}{F(d_t)}\bar{\tau} \tag{16}E[β^​1​]=F(dt​)F(d∗)​τˉ(16)

so the estimate is scaled down by the share of truly affected units in the treated ring. Assumption 4 is very demanding and is unlikely to be met unless prior theory dictates dtd_tdt​; the paper's examples are Currie et al. (2015), who use scientific evidence on the maximum spread of local pollutants, and Marcus (2021), who uses the plume length of petroleum smoke. Earlier applied papers use several rings to trace effects at different distances. The paper notes that those rings are chosen ad hoc, that the approach still requires effects to be zero beyond the outermost treated ring, and that it invites specification searching. It does not state a separate proposition for the multi-ring regression.

Nonparametric Estimator

Partition-based estimators split the support of a covariate, here Disti\text{Dist}_iDisti​, into quantile-spaced intervals and estimate the conditional expectation separately within each interval as a polynomial of degree kkk in the covariate. For a given outer distance dcd_cdc​ the sample is D={i:Disti≤dc}\mathcal{D}=\{i:\text{Dist}_i\leq d_c\}D={i:Disti​≤dc​}, and it is split into LLL intervals. For j∈{1,…,L}j\in\{1,\ldots,L\}j∈{1,…,L} the jjj-th interval is:

Dj≡{i:Fn−1(j−1L)≤Disti<Fn−1(jL)}(17)\mathcal{D}_j\equiv\left\{i:F_n^{-1}\left(\frac{j-1}{L}\right)\leq\text{Dist}_i<F_n^{-1}\left(\frac{j}{L}\right)\right\} \tag{17}Dj​≡{i:Fn−1​(Lj−1​)≤Disti​<Fn−1​(Lj​)}(17)

where FnF_nFn​ is the empirical distribution of Dist\text{Dist}Dist. The paper uses a polynomial of degree zero, k=0k=0k=0, a constant within each interval, which has no asymptotic cost because the approximation can be made arbitrarily good by increasing either the number of intervals or the polynomial order. The constants are the bin means:

ΔY‾j≡1nj∑i∈DjΔYit(18)\overline{\Delta Y}_j\equiv\frac{1}{n_j}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_j}\Delta Y_{it} \tag{18}ΔYj​≡nj​1​i∈Dj​∑​ΔYit​(18)

where nj≈n/Ln_j\approx n/Lnj​≈n/L is the number of units in bin Dj\mathcal{D}_jDj​. The estimator of E[ΔYit∣Disti]\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta Y_{it}\mid\text{Dist}_i\right]E[ΔYit​∣Disti​] is the step function:

ΔYit^=∑j=1L1i∈DjΔY‾j(19)\widehat{\Delta Y_{it}}=\sum_{j=1}^L\mathbf{1}_{i\in\mathcal{D}_j}\overline{\Delta Y}_j \tag{19}ΔYit​​=j=1∑L​1i∈Dj​​ΔYj​(19)

which approaches the conditional expectation uniformly as the number of intervals goes to infinity. Under Local Parallel Trends:

E[ΔYit∣Dist=d]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dist=d]+λ(20)\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta Y_{it}\mid\text{Dist}=d\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}=d\right]+\lambda \tag{20}E[ΔYit​∣Dist=d]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dist=d]+λ(20)

Assumption 5 (dtd_tdt​ is within dcd_cdc​) holds for a distance dcd_cdc​ if there exists a distance dtd_tdt​ with 0<dt<dc0<d_t<d_c0<dt​<dc​ such that Assumption 4 holds and F(dc)−F(dt)>0F(d_c)-F(d_t)>0F(dc​)−F(dt​)>0. As L→∞L\to\inftyL→∞ the left end-point of the last bin exceeds dtd_tdt​, so that τ(Dist)=0\tau(\text{Dist})=0τ(Dist)=0 in DL\mathcal{D}_LDL​ and the mean of the last ring estimates λ\lambdaλ (the paper once calls this ring Dk\mathcal{D}_kDk​). The estimate of the curve on interval jjj is:

τ^j≡ΔY‾j−ΔY‾L(21)\hat{\tau}_j\equiv\overline{\Delta Y}_j-\overline{\Delta Y}_L \tag{21}τ^j​≡ΔYj​−ΔYL​(21)

and the τ^j\hat{\tau}_jτ^j​ are plotted over their intervals. Proposition 2 (Consistency of Nonparametric Estimator): given that units follow the model above and dcd_cdc​ satisfies Local Parallel Trends and Assumption 5, as nnn and L→∞L\to\inftyL→∞:

τ^≡∑j=1Lτ^j1i∈Dj→unifτ(Dist)(22)\hat{\tau}\equiv\sum_{j=1}^L\hat{\tau}_j\mathbf{1}_{i\in\mathcal{D}_j}\to^{unif}\tau(\text{Dist}) \tag{22}τ^≡j=1∑L​τ^j​1i∈Dj​​→unifτ(Dist)(22)

(the paper prints the sum over i=1i=1i=1). The proof has three steps. First, L→∞L\to\inftyL→∞ implies dt≤Fn−1(L−1L)d_t\leq F_n^{-1}\left(\frac{L-1}{L}\right)dt​≤Fn−1​(LL−1​) by Assumption 5, so that ΔY‾L→pλ\overline{\Delta Y}_L\to^p\lambdaΔYL​→pλ as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞. Second, by Local Parallel Trends and the model:

τ^j=ΔY‾j−ΔY‾L→pE[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj]+λ−λ=E[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj](23)\hat{\tau}_j=\overline{\Delta Y}_j-\overline{\Delta Y}_L\to^p\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}\in\mathcal{D}_j\right]+\lambda-\lambda=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}\in\mathcal{D}_j\right] \tag{23}τ^j​=ΔYj​−ΔYL​→pE[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj​]+λ−λ=E[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj​](23)

Third, as L→∞L\to\inftyL→∞ and n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞ each Dj\mathcal{D}_jDj​ shrinks to a single point djd_jdj​, so τ^j\hat{\tau}_jτ^j​ converges in probability to the value of the curve at djd_jdj​ and the step function converges pointwise. Uniform convergence and the smoothness conditions it requires are taken from Cattaneo, Farrell and Feng; the paper states no rate. With a fixed LLL in a finite sample there is a fixed set of estimates with the last one equal to zero by construction, and each τ^j\hat{\tau}_jτ^j​ is approximately the average treatment effect within the interval Dj\mathcal{D}_jDj​.

The gain has a price. The estimator no longer identifies the curve under the milder Average Parallel Trends assumption, so the researcher must argue explicitly that every unit within the dcd_cdc​ ring is subject to the same trend. This is plausible at a very local level and not for larger units such as counties. The assumption is not testable, but the plot gives visual evidence: effects usually stop well before dcd_cdc​, so the estimates τ^j\hat{\tau}_jτ^j​ with jjj close to LLL should be centered at zero if trends are common. This is not a formal test, since τ(Dist)\tau(\text{Dist})τ(Dist) and λ(Dist)\lambda(\text{Dist})λ(Dist) could cancel exactly, but that is a knife-edge case. A curve that shrinks with distance also strengthens a causal reading, like a dose-response function, and a curve that changes sign (a bus stop that hurts immediate neighbours and helps homes within walking distance) explains an average effect near zero.

Number of Rings and Inference

The number of bins is chosen as the data-driven optimal L∗L^*L∗ derived by Cattaneo, Crump, Farrell and Feng. A larger LLL lets the conditional expectation vary more across values of Dist\text{Dist}Dist and lowers the bias, but raises the variance; the balance depends on the shape and curvature of τ(Dist)\tau(\text{Dist})τ(Dist), which is estimated from the data. The paper refers to that work for the formula and prints none. The rings are then the quantiles of the data. Because the rings are themselves estimated, the cited inference results account for the first-stage estimation of the quantiles. The data-driven choice removes the incentive to pre-test rings in search of a significant result. Since the estimator is a difference of two bin means, the standard error of τ^j\hat{\tau}_jτ^j​ is:

σj2+σL2(24)\sqrt{\sigma_j^2+\sigma_L^2} \tag{24}σj2​+σL2​​(24)

where σj\sigma_jσj​ is the robust standard error of the conditional mean of bin jjj recommended by Cattaneo, Crump, Farrell and Feng and produced by the Stata/R package binsreg. Inference uses the estimated t-statistic with the standard normal distribution, that is, pointwise intervals for each ring; the paper does not construct uniform confidence bands. It argues that no adjustment for spatial correlation is needed, because under Assumption 2 the error term is uncorrelated with distance.

Three remarks qualify the method. Remark 1 (overall average effect): since the bins are quantiles, a simple average of the significant τ^j\hat{\tau}_jτ^j​ gives a back-of-the-envelope overall effect, but inference on it is not possible, because the number of significant rings changes in repeated sampling and this model selection invalidates standard inference (Leeb and Potscher 2005). A possible solution is sample splitting, with one half of the data determining the inner ring and the other half estimating the average effect, at the cost of a large sample. Remark 2 (covariates): covariates can be included with valid inference, but parallel trends must then hold conditional on the covariate vector XXX, that is, neighborhood shocks must be common across values of XiX_iXi​. Remark 3 (choosing dcd_cdc​): the outer distance must still be specified. One possibility is to apply the estimator to the pre-treatment periods t=−2,−1t=-2,-1t=−2,−1 with a large dcd_cdc​. These estimates approximate λ(Dist)\lambda(\text{Dist})λ(Dist), and the largest distance over which they remain flat is a good choice of dcd_cdc​. This is the pre-trend counterpart of the method.

Monte Carlo Evidence

Appendix B compares the ring method with the nonparametric method in 2000 simulations. Units are drawn on the unit disc (the paper says unit circle) in two periods from the data-generating process of Diamond and McQuade (2019):

pit=1+τ(Disti)1t=1+βLatLati+λ1t=1+βLonLoni+εit(25)p_{it}=1+\tau(\text{Dist}_i)\mathbf{1}_{t=1}+\beta_{\text{Lat}}\text{Lat}_i+\lambda\mathbf{1}_{t=1}+\beta_{\text{Lon}}\text{Lon}_i+\varepsilon_{it} \tag{25}pit​=1+τ(Disti​)1t=1​+βLat​Lati​+λ1t=1​+βLon​Loni​+εit​(25)

where (Lati,Loni)(\text{Lat}_i,\text{Lon}_i)(Lati​,Loni​) are the coordinates of unit iii, βLat∼N(0,0.036)\beta_{\text{Lat}}\sim N(0,0.036)βLat​∼N(0,0.036) and βLon∼N(0,0.036)\beta_{\text{Lon}}\sim N(0,0.036)βLon​∼N(0,0.036) determine how price levels vary over space, λ∼N(0,0.025)\lambda\sim N(0,0.025)λ∼N(0,0.025) is the constant common trend and εit∼N(0,0.036)\varepsilon_{it}\sim N(0,0.036)εit​∼N(0,0.036) is an idiosyncratic error. The first is flat, the case most favourable to rings. The second is the smoothly declining positive curve of Diamond and McQuade (2019). The third starts negative, turns positive and returns to zero by 0.8; the paper describes the sign change as occurring around 0.3 and the average as near zero, although the printed formula changes sign at about 0.14 and has a positive average. The fourth affects only units very close to treatment. Three estimators are compared: two rings {(0,0.6],(0.6,1]}\{(0,0.6],(0.6,1]\}{(0,0.6],(0.6,1]}, three rings (printed as {(0,0.3],(0.3,0.6],(0.5,1]}\{(0,0.3],(0.3,0.6],(0.5,1]\}{(0,0.3],(0.3,0.6],(0.5,1]}, where the last interval presumably should start at 0.6) and the nonparametric estimator. The paper describes the ring specifications as satisfying the correct maximum treatment distance, which is not known in practice, although the printed inner cutoff of 0.6 does not coincide with the reach of any of the four curves. Performance is measured by the prediction error at each data point:

υi≡τ^(Disti)−τ(Disti)(27)\upsilon_i\equiv\hat{\tau}(\text{Dist}_i)-\tau(\text{Dist}_i) \tag{27}υi​≡τ^(Disti​)−τ(Disti​)(27)

summarized by the mean squared error E^(υi2)\hat{E}(\upsilon_i^2)E^(υi2​) and the mean absolute error E^(∣υi∣)\hat{E}(|\upsilon_i|)E^(∣υi​∣) over observations with positive treatment effects, and by the bias of the predicted effect at 0.4 miles. Each metric is divided by its value for the nonparametric estimator, so values above one mean that rings do worse.

  • Flat curve τ1\tau_1τ1​: rings do better on every metric and at every sample size. The relative mean squared error of two rings falls from 0.33 at n=250n=250n=250 to 0.12 at n=5000n=5000n=5000 (three rings: 0.46 to 0.16), because wide rings approximate a flat curve accurately while the nonparametric estimator carries sampling noise.

  • Smooth curve τ2\tau_2τ2​: the relative mean squared error of two rings rises from 0.81 at n=250n=250n=250 to 3.81 at n=5000n=5000n=5000 and that of three rings from 0.56 to 1.15; the relative bias at 0.4 miles at n=5000n=5000n=5000 is 4.32 and 2.22.

  • Sign-changing curve τ3\tau_3τ3​: the relative mean squared error rises from 0.62 to 2.18 for two rings and from 0.72 to 2.17 for three rings. For τ2\tau_2τ2​ and τ3\tau_3τ3​ rings do better on mean squared error in small samples, though not on every metric, and by 5000 observations the nonparametric method does better on all three metrics.

  • Hyper-local curve τ4\tau_4τ4​: the nonparametric method does at least as well already in small samples (relative mean squared error of two rings 1.57 at n=250n=250n=250 and 6.96 at n=5000n=5000n=5000; of three rings 0.93 and 3.37), because it isolates the large effect very close to treatment while wide rings average over many unaffected units.

The appendix text attributes the last result, and the overall conclusion, to the rings method; the table shows that the nonparametric method is meant. With at least a few thousand observations the nonparametric method performs better in most settings, except when the treatment effect curve is approximately flat.

Application: Sex Offender Arrivals and Home Prices

Linden and Rockoff (2008) estimate the effect of a registered sex offender moving into a neighborhood on home prices with the ring method. Treated homes are within one tenth of a mile of the offender's home and control homes are between one tenth and one third of a mile away. They argue that within such a narrow area trends are common and that the exact location of a home purchase is hard to time with hyper-local shocks. There is little prior basis for the treated distance. The original paper chooses it from kernel estimates of the price gradient in the year before and the year after arrival, by eyeballing where the two curves meet. Re-estimating that figure with bandwidths of 0.025, 0.075 (the published one) and 0.125 moves the apparent meeting point from about 0.1 to about 0.15 and about 0.2 miles, so the evidence for 0.1 miles depends on the bandwidth.

The standard approach is the proposed estimator with two rings, D1\mathcal{D}_1D1​ for homes between 0 and 0.1 miles and D2\mathcal{D}_2D2​ for homes between 0.1 and 0.3 miles, that is, τ^j\hat{\tau}_jτ^j​ for j=1,2j=1,2j=1,2. It gives an average decline in home values of about 7.5 percent after arrival for homes within 0.1 miles, according to the text; the bar plotted in the corresponding figure panel sits near −0.06-0.06−0.06 log points. That homes between 0.1 and 0.3 miles are unaffected is assumed, not tested. The data are a repeated cross-section of home sales and not a panel, so first differences cannot be formed. Identification then needs the extra assumption that the composition of homes at a given distance does not change over time, and separate nonparametric estimators are computed before and after arrival and subtracted; the details are in the online appendix.

The nonparametric curve, with about two dozen data-chosen rings between 0 and 0.3 miles, differs in two ways. First, homes in the two closest rings, within a few hundred feet, are the most affected, with an estimated decline of around 20 percent, while homes slightly further away but still inside the original treated ring show no statistically significant effect. The published estimate of τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ is therefore attenuated towards zero by homes with little or no effect and understates the effect on the closest homes. The effect shrinks with distance, which supports a causal interpretation. Second, beyond 0.1 miles the estimated curve is consistently centered at zero, so each ring has the same estimated trend as the outermost ring. This is suggestive evidence that homes in the neighborhood share a common trend, the informal check of Local Parallel Trends. The paper relates the result to difference-in-differences with a continuous treatment (Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna 2021): Local Parallel Trends is the analogue of common trends at different doses, and the curve can be estimated here because τ(Dist)\tau(\text{Dist})τ(Dist) is assumed homogeneous across units.

This is the unit-level outcome model, the primitive of the whole note. YitY_{it}Yit​ is the outcome (for example the log price of home iii) in period t∈{0,1}t\in\{0,1\}t∈{0,1}, and treatment happens at one point in space between the two periods. μi\mu_iμi​ is a time-invariant unit effect: it captures everything permanent about the unit, including permanent differences in levels across locations. λi\lambda_iλi​ is the change in the untreated outcome of unit iii between the two periods, its own counterfactual trend. τi\tau_iτi​ is the treatment effect of unit iii; a unit that is not affected has τi=0\tau_i=0τi​=0. uitu_{it}uit​ is a transitory shock.

Nothing is restricted at this stage: every unit has its own level, its own trend and its own effect. The potential outcomes implied by the model are

Yi1(0)=μi+λi+ui1,Yi1(1)=Yi1(0)+τi,Yi0=μi+ui0Y_{i1}(0)=\mu_i+\lambda_i+u_{i1},\qquad Y_{i1}(1)=Y_{i1}(0)+\tau_i,\qquad Y_{i0}=\mu_i+u_{i0}Yi1​(0)=μi​+λi​+ui1​,Yi1​(1)=Yi1​(0)+τi​,Yi0​=μi​+ui0​

so τi\tau_iτi​ and λi\lambda_iλi​ always appear together in period 1 and only their sum τi+λi\tau_i+\lambda_iτi​+λi​ can be learned from one unit. There is no treatment indicator: all units are potentially exposed, and exposure differs only through the distance Disti\text{Dist}_iDisti​. This is why the note needs assumptions on how λ\lambdaλ and τ\tauτ vary with distance, introduced through equation (2), and why the target in equation (5) is an effect on the affected units instead of an effect on the treated. The model also rules out anticipation (no effect at t=0t=0t=0) and uses only two periods.

The natural reading, which the paper states in words for τ\tauτ ("the average effect of treatment at a given distance"), is that the systematic part is the conditional mean:

z(d)≡E[zi∣Disti=d],z∈{τ,λ}z(d)\equiv\mathbb{E}\left[z_i\mid\text{Dist}_i=d\right],\qquad z\in\{\tau,\lambda\}z(d)≡E[zi​∣Disti​=d],z∈{τ,λ}

The data identify the sum of the two curves at each distance and nothing more: for any function ggg, the pair τ(d)+g(d)\tau(d)+g(d)τ(d)+g(d) and λ(d)−g(d)\lambda(d)-g(d)λ(d)−g(d) fits the data equally well. Equations (7), (8) and (10) are the restrictions that separate them.

Assumption 2 (Local Parallel Trends) says that the counterfactual trend curve is flat on the interval of distances from zero to dˉ\bar{d}dˉ: every unit within dˉ\bar{d}dˉ of the treatment location would, on average, have experienced the same change in the outcome without treatment. It is a restriction on the curve λ(d)\lambda(d)λ(d), the conditional mean of λi\lambda_iλi​, so individual trends may still differ through λ~i\tilde{\lambda}_iλ~i​. The word "positive" excludes only the treatment point itself.

What it buys: applied at dˉ=dc\bar{d}=d_cdˉ=dc​ it turns the unidentified sum of equation (6) into a curve plus a constant, equation (9), so that the shape of the effect curve is identified and only its level is not. It is the formal version of the usual verbal argument that homes in a small neighborhood share the same shocks. What it rules out: a location of treatment chosen in response to very local trends, trends that vary smoothly with distance inside the sample (a gradient towards a city centre that happens to coincide with distance to treatment), and sorting of units towards or away from the treatment location that changes composition between periods.

It is stronger than the usual difference-in-differences assumption, equation (8), which only requires equal average trends in two rings. The stronger form is what the nonparametric estimator of equations (21) and (22) needs, because that estimator compares every small ring with the last one. It is not testable, but it has a visible implication: estimates for rings beyond the reach of the effect should be centered at zero.

Assumption 3 (Average Parallel Trends) is the standard parallel trends condition for the two groups of the ring method defined in equation (11): the mean counterfactual trend of the inner ring equals that of the outer ring. The paper writes it with the symbols λd\lambda_dλd​ and ddd; the note's version with λ(Disti)\lambda(\text{Dist}_i)λ(Disti​) and the random variable Disti\text{Dist}_iDisti​ in the conditioning event is the correct reading, since an expectation over rings must be taken over the distribution of unit distances. By iterated expectations it is the same as equality of the means of the unit-level trends λi\lambda_iλi​ in the two rings.

It is implied by Local Parallel Trends, equation (7), when that holds for dˉ=dc\bar{d}=d_cdˉ=dc​: if λ(d)=λ\lambda(d)=\lambdaλ(d)=λ for all distances up to dcd_cdc​, then

E[λ(Disti)∣0≤Disti≤dt]=λ=E[λ(Disti)∣dt<Disti≤dc]\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(\text{Dist}_i)\mid0\leq\text{Dist}_i\leq d_t\right]=\lambda=\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(\text{Dist}_i)\mid d_t<\text{Dist}_i\leq d_c\right]E[λ(Disti​)∣0≤Disti​≤dt​]=λ=E[λ(Disti​)∣dt​<Disti​≤dc​]

The converse fails. A trend curve that is not flat can have equal ring averages for one particular pair of distances, for example a curve that dips and recovers, and the equality would then be lost if either distance were changed. The condition is thus specific to the pair (dt,dc)(d_t,d_c)(dt​,dc​) and depends on the distribution FFF through the weights. It is sufficient for the ring estimator, where it removes the second term of equation (13) and gives equation (14), but it is not sufficient for the many-ring estimator of equation (22).

Start from the first-difference equation (6) and restrict attention to units in the sample D\mathcal{D}D, those with Disti≤dc\text{Dist}_i\leq d_cDisti​≤dc​. Suppose Local Parallel Trends, equation (7), holds with dˉ=dc\bar{d}=d_cdˉ=dc​. Then the trend curve takes one common value on the sample; call it λ\lambdaλ:

λ(Disti)=λfor all i∈D\lambda(\text{Dist}_i)=\lambda\quad\text{for all }i\in\mathcal{D}λ(Disti​)=λfor all i∈D

Substituting into equation (6):

ΔYit=τ(Disti)+λ+Δεit\Delta Y_{it}=\tau(\text{Dist}_i)+\lambda+\Delta\varepsilon_{it}ΔYit​=τ(Disti​)+λ+Δεit​

Taking conditional expectations, the regression function of the change on distance is

E[ΔYit∣Disti=d]=τ(d)+λ,d≤dc\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta Y_{it}\mid\text{Dist}_i=d\right]=\tau(d)+\lambda,\qquad d\leq d_cE[ΔYit​∣Disti​=d]=τ(d)+λ,d≤dc​

The left-hand side is identified from the data, so the effect curve is identified up to the additive constant λ\lambdaλ. Differences of the curve between any two distances are identified without further assumptions:

E[ΔYit∣Disti=d]−E[ΔYit∣Disti=d′]=τ(d)−τ(d′)\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta Y_{it}\mid\text{Dist}_i=d\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta Y_{it}\mid\text{Dist}_i=d'\right]=\tau(d)-\tau(d')E[ΔYit​∣Disti​=d]−E[ΔYit​∣Disti​=d′]=τ(d)−τ(d′)

To recover the level one needs a distance d′d'd′ at which the effect is known to be zero. Equation (10) supplies it for the ring method, and Assumption 5 supplies it for the nonparametric estimator.

Assumption 4 (Correct dtd_tdt​) states that the researcher's inner distance is exactly the reach of the treatment. Part (i) has two halves. The second half, zero effect beyond dtd_tdt​, makes the outer ring a clean control group: under equation (9) its mean change is λ\lambdaλ. The first half, a strictly positive effect at every distance up to dtd_tdt​, makes the inner ring coincide with the set of affected units, so that the inner-ring mean of the curve equals τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ of equation (5). Part (ii) says that a positive share of units lies between dtd_tdt​ and dcd_cdc​, so the control ring is not empty and the regression of equation (12) can be run.

Together the two halves define a knife-edge: if effects end at d∗d^{*}d∗, only dt=d∗d_t=d^{*}dt​=d∗ satisfies the assumption. A smaller dtd_tdt​ violates the second half and contaminates the control ring; a larger dtd_tdt​ violates the first half and dilutes the treated ring, with the result in equation (16). The curve may be discontinuous at dtd_tdt​, as in the paper's illustrative figure, where it falls from about 0.28 to zero at 0.75 miles.

The sign restriction is written for a positive effect. For a negative effect read it as non-zero. A curve that crosses zero strictly inside its reach, such as τ3\tau_3τ3​ in equation (26), does not satisfy the first half literally at the crossing point, which is harmless because a single distance has probability zero. The assumption is used in equation (15) and is weakened to mere existence of such a distance in Assumption 5.

These are the two groups of the ring method. Dt\mathcal{D}_tDt​ is the disc of radius dtd_tdt​ around the treatment location, the "treated" ring, and Dc\mathcal{D}_cDc​ is the annulus between dtd_tdt​ and dcd_cdc​, the "control" ring. Units further away than dcd_cdc​ are dropped. The sets are disjoint and their union is the estimation sample D\mathcal{D}D, the units within dcd_cdc​. In terms of the distribution function of distance, the population shares are

Pr⁡(i∈Dt)=F(dt),Pr⁡(i∈Dc)=F(dc)−F(dt)\Pr\left(i\in\mathcal{D}_t\right)=F(d_t),\qquad\Pr\left(i\in\mathcal{D}_c\right)=F(d_c)-F(d_t)Pr(i∈Dt​)=F(dt​),Pr(i∈Dc​)=F(dc​)−F(dt​)

and the share of the treated ring within the sample is the ratio of F(dt)F(d_t)F(dt​) to F(dc)F(d_c)F(dc​). These shares are the weights in every ring average that follows.

Both distances are chosen by the researcher. Membership in Dt\mathcal{D}_tDt​ is a label, not a fact about who is affected: whether the labelled group coincides with the affected units is the content of Assumption 4 in equation (10). The outer distance matters as well, since it must be small enough for parallel trends, equation (7) or (8), and large enough to leave units beyond the reach of the effect. In the application the distances are 0.1 and about 0.3 miles; in the paper's illustrative figure they are 0.75 and 1.5 miles in the correct specification. The groups enter the regression of equation (12) and the decomposition of equation (13).

This is the estimating equation of the ring method: a regression of the unit-level change on a constant and an indicator for the inner ring, run on units within dcd_cdc​. Because the regressor is a single indicator the least squares coefficients are group means. β^0\hat{\beta}_0β^​0​ is the mean change in the control ring and

β^1=1nt∑i∈DtΔYit−1nc∑i∈DcΔYit\hat{\beta}_1=\frac{1}{n_t}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_t}\Delta Y_{it}-\frac{1}{n_c}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_c}\Delta Y_{it}β^​1​=nt​1​i∈Dt​∑​ΔYit​−nc​1​i∈Dc​∑​ΔYit​

where ntn_tnt​ and ncn_cnc​ are the numbers of units in the two rings. This is a difference-in-differences: a difference over time inside each ring, then a difference across rings. With two periods it is numerically the same as a regression of the level YitY_{it}Yit​ on unit fixed effects, a period-1 indicator and the interaction of the inner-ring indicator with period 1.

The error uitu_{it}uit​ here is the regression error and is not the shock of equation (1); the paper reuses the letter. Comparing with equation (9), the regression is correctly specified only if the curve is a step function equal to a constant inside dtd_tdt​ and zero outside, in which case β0=λ\beta_0=\lambdaβ0​=λ and β1\beta_1β1​ is the height of the step. In general it is a projection, and what β^1\hat{\beta}_1β^​1​ estimates is given by equations (13) to (16). The identifying variation is cross-sectional variation in distance to one treatment location, used only through the two-group split. Everything about the shape of the effect within a ring is averaged out.

Start from the least squares solution of equation (12), the difference between the mean changes of the two rings. Condition on the distances of the sampled units, so that ring membership is fixed, and use random sampling (Assumption 1): each ring mean is an average of independent draws from the distribution of the change given membership in that ring. Hence

E[β^1]=E[ΔYit∣Dt]−E[ΔYit∣Dc]\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\beta}_1\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta Y_{it}\mid\mathcal{D}_t\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta Y_{it}\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right]E[β^​1​]=E[ΔYit​∣Dt​]−E[ΔYit​∣Dc​]

which is the first line. Substitute the first-difference equation (6) into each conditional mean and use linearity:

E[β^1]=E[τ(Dist)+λ(Dist)+Δεit∣Dt]−E[τ(Dist)+λ(Dist)+Δεit∣Dc]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dt]−E[τ(Dist)∣Dc]+E[λ(Dist)∣Dt]−E[λ(Dist)∣Dc]+E[Δεit∣Dt]−E[Δεit∣Dc]\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\beta}_1\right]&=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})+\lambda(\text{Dist})+\Delta\varepsilon_{it}\mid\mathcal{D}_t\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})+\lambda(\text{Dist})+\Delta\varepsilon_{it}\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right]\\ &=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_t\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right]\\ &\quad+\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_t\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right]\\ &\quad+\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta\varepsilon_{it}\mid\mathcal{D}_t\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta\varepsilon_{it}\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right] \end{aligned}E[β^​1​]​=E[τ(Dist)+λ(Dist)+Δεit​∣Dt​]−E[τ(Dist)+λ(Dist)+Δεit​∣Dc​]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dt​]−E[τ(Dist)∣Dc​]+E[λ(Dist)∣Dt​]−E[λ(Dist)∣Dc​]+E[Δεit​∣Dt​]−E[Δεit​∣Dc​]​

The last line is zero. Ring membership is a function of distance alone, so by iterated expectations and the mean independence established under equation (4),

E[Δεit∣Dt]=E[E[Δεit∣Disti]∣Disti≤dt]=0\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta\varepsilon_{it}\mid\mathcal{D}_t\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta\varepsilon_{it}\mid\text{Dist}_i\right]\mid\text{Dist}_i\leq d_t\right]=0E[Δεit​∣Dt​]=E[E[Δεit​∣Disti​]∣Disti​≤dt​]=0

and in the same way for the control ring. What remains is the target: a difference in mean treatment effects between the rings plus a difference in mean counterfactual trends. No identifying assumption has been used. This step needs mean independence of the error from distance; the paper's phrase "uncorrelated with distance" is not literally enough, because a ring indicator is a nonlinear function of distance.

The decomposition can be regrouped into the three objects of interest. Adding and subtracting τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ:

E[β^1]−τˉ={E[τ(Dist)∣Dt]−τˉ}−E[τ(Dist)∣Dc]+{E[λ(Dist)∣Dt]−E[λ(Dist)∣Dc]}\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\beta}_1\right]-\bar{\tau}=\left\{\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_t\right]-\bar{\tau}\right\}-\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right]+\left\{\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_t\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right]\right\}E[β^​1​]−τˉ={E[τ(Dist)∣Dt​]−τˉ}−E[τ(Dist)∣Dc​]+{E[λ(Dist)∣Dt​]−E[λ(Dist)∣Dc​]}

The first brace is non-zero when the inner ring is not the set of affected units, the middle term is the average effect on affected units wrongly placed in the control ring, and the last brace is the differential trend.

Start from equation (13) and show that the trend term vanishes under either assumption.

Under Average Parallel Trends for the pair (dt,dc)(d_t,d_c)(dt​,dc​), equation (8) is exactly the statement that the two ring means of the trend curve are equal, since conditioning on Dt\mathcal{D}_tDt​ and Dc\mathcal{D}_cDc​ is conditioning on the two distance intervals of equation (11):

E[λ(Dist)∣Dt]−E[λ(Dist)∣Dc]=0\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_t\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right]=0E[λ(Dist)∣Dt​]−E[λ(Dist)∣Dc​]=0

Under Local Parallel Trends for dcd_cdc​, equation (7) gives a common value λ\lambdaλ at every distance in the sample, so each ring mean equals that constant:

E[λ(Dist)∣Dt]−E[λ(Dist)∣Dc]=λ−λ=0\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_t\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right]=\lambda-\lambda=0E[λ(Dist)∣Dt​]−E[λ(Dist)∣Dc​]=λ−λ=0

In both cases equation (13) reduces to

E[β^1]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dt]−E[τ(Dist)∣Dc]\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\beta}_1\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_t\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right]E[β^​1​]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dt​]−E[τ(Dist)∣Dc​]

Written with the distribution of distance, the two means are

E[τ(Dist)∣Dt]=1F(dt)∫0dtτ(d) dF(d),E[τ(Dist)∣Dc]=1F(dc)−F(dt)∫dtdcτ(d) dF(d)\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_t\right]=\frac{1}{F(d_t)}\int_0^{d_t}\tau(d)\,dF(d),\qquad\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right]=\frac{1}{F(d_c)-F(d_t)}\int_{d_t}^{d_c}\tau(d)\,dF(d)E[τ(Dist)∣Dt​]=F(dt​)1​∫0dt​​τ(d)dF(d),E[τ(Dist)∣Dc​]=F(dc​)−F(dt​)1​∫dt​dc​​τ(d)dF(d)

Parallel trends alone therefore delivers a contrast of two ring averages of the curve, not τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ. If effects end at d∗d^{*}d∗ and the inner ring is too narrow, dt<d∗d_t<d^{*}dt​<d∗, the expression becomes

E[β^1]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dist≤dt]−F(d∗)−F(dt)F(dc)−F(dt) E[τ(Dist)∣dt<Dist≤d∗]\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\beta}_1\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}\leq d_t\right]-\frac{F(d^{*})-F(d_t)}{F(d_c)-F(d_t)}\,\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid d_t<\text{Dist}\leq d^{*}\right]E[β^​1​]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dist≤dt​]−F(dc​)−F(dt​)F(d∗)−F(dt​)​E[τ(Dist)∣dt​<Dist≤d∗]

For a decreasing curve the first term exceeds τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ, because only the closest units are kept, while the second term is subtracted, so the sign of the bias is ambiguous. This is the note's "too narrow" case. In the paper's illustrative figure the net result is an estimate of 0.81 against 0.73 for the correct ring. The "too wide" case is equation (16).

Start from equation (14), which holds under Local Parallel Trends for dcd_cdc​. Assumption 4, equation (10), says that the curve is zero at every distance above dtd_tdt​. All units of the control ring have distances above dtd_tdt​, so

E[τ(Dist)∣Dc]=E[τ(Dist)∣dt<Dist≤dc]=0\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid d_t<\text{Dist}\leq d_c\right]=0E[τ(Dist)∣Dc​]=E[τ(Dist)∣dt​<Dist≤dc​]=0

The same assumption says that the curve is strictly positive at every distance up to dtd_tdt​. Hence the set of distances with a positive effect is exactly the inner ring, including for units outside the sample, where the effect is zero as well:

{τ(Disti)>0}={Disti≤dt}={i∈Dt}\left\{\tau(\text{Dist}_i)>0\right\}=\left\{\text{Dist}_i\leq d_t\right\}=\left\{i\in\mathcal{D}_t\right\}{τ(Disti​)>0}={Disti​≤dt​}={i∈Dt​}

Use this in the definition of the target parameter, equation (5), split the unit effect with equation (2), and apply iterated expectations to the idiosyncratic part:

τˉ=E[τi∣Disti≤dt]=E[τ(Disti)∣Disti≤dt]+E[E[τ~i∣Disti]∣Disti≤dt]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dt]\begin{aligned} \bar{\tau}&=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau_i\mid\text{Dist}_i\leq d_t\right]\\ &=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist}_i)\mid\text{Dist}_i\leq d_t\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{\tau}_i\mid\text{Dist}_i\right]\mid\text{Dist}_i\leq d_t\right]\\ &=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_t\right] \end{aligned}τˉ​=E[τi​∣Disti​≤dt​]=E[τ(Disti​)∣Disti​≤dt​]+E[E[τ~i​∣Disti​]∣Disti​≤dt​]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dt​]​

Combining the two results in equation (14):

E[β^1]=τˉ−0=τˉ\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\beta}_1\right]=\bar{\tau}-0=\bar{\tau}E[β^​1​]=τˉ−0=τˉ

The ring estimator is unbiased for the average effect on the affected units. The paper states this part with Local Parallel Trends; the argument shows that Average Parallel Trends for (dt,dc)(d_t,d_c)(dt​,dc​) is enough, since only equation (14) is used. The paper's proof mentions only the zero mean in the control ring; the second step, that the inner-ring mean equals τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ, uses the first half of Assumption 4(i) and is supplied by the note.

This equation is the note's own and is not in the paper. The assumptions are: (a) parallel trends, either equation (7) for dcd_cdc​ or equation (8) for the pair (dt,dc)(d_t,d_c)(dt​,dc​), so that equation (14) applies; (b) the true reach of the effect is d∗d^{*}d∗, meaning that d∗d^{*}d∗ satisfies part (i) of equation (10); (c) the chosen inner distance is too wide, with d∗<dt<dcd^{*}<d_t<d_cd∗<dt​<dc​; (d) FFF is the population distribution function of distance, so that F(d)F(d)F(d) is the probability that a unit lies within ddd of treatment and F(d∗)>0F(d^{*})>0F(d∗)>0.

Start from equation (14). Since dt>d∗d_t>d^{*}dt​>d∗, all control units lie beyond the reach of the effect:

E[τ(Dist)∣Dc]=0\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\mathcal{D}_c\right]=0E[τ(Dist)∣Dc​]=0

For the treated ring, split it at d∗d^{*}d∗ with the law of total expectation:

E[τ(Dist)∣Dist≤dt]=Pr⁡(Dist≤d∗∣Dist≤dt)E[τ(Dist)∣Dist≤d∗]+Pr⁡(d∗<Dist≤dt∣Dist≤dt)E[τ(Dist)∣d∗<Dist≤dt]\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}\leq d_t\right]&=\Pr\left(\text{Dist}\leq d^{*}\mid\text{Dist}\leq d_t\right)\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}\leq d^{*}\right]\\ &\quad+\Pr\left(d^{*}<\text{Dist}\leq d_t\mid\text{Dist}\leq d_t\right)\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid d^{*}<\text{Dist}\leq d_t\right] \end{aligned}E[τ(Dist)∣Dist≤dt​]​=Pr(Dist≤d∗∣Dist≤dt​)E[τ(Dist)∣Dist≤d∗]+Pr(d∗<Dist≤dt​∣Dist≤dt​)E[τ(Dist)∣d∗<Dist≤dt​]​

The second expectation is zero because the curve is zero above d∗d^{*}d∗. The first expectation is τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ, by the argument of equation (15) applied to d∗d^{*}d∗: the affected units are exactly those with distance at most d∗d^{*}d∗. The conditional probability is a ratio of distribution functions:

Pr⁡(Dist≤d∗∣Dist≤dt)=F(d∗)F(dt)\Pr\left(\text{Dist}\leq d^{*}\mid\text{Dist}\leq d_t\right)=\frac{F(d^{*})}{F(d_t)}Pr(Dist≤d∗∣Dist≤dt​)=F(dt​)F(d∗)​

Therefore

E[β^1]=F(d∗)F(dt)τˉ\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\beta}_1\right]=\frac{F(d^{*})}{F(d_t)}\bar{\tau}E[β^​1​]=F(dt​)F(d∗)​τˉ

The factor is the share of truly affected units in the treated ring. It lies strictly between zero and one whenever some units are located between d∗d^{*}d∗ and dtd_tdt​, so the estimate keeps the sign of τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ and is attenuated towards zero. Here τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ averages over all affected units in the population, those within d∗d^{*}d∗, all of which are inside the sample. The ratio is unchanged if FFF is replaced by the distribution of distance within the sample D\mathcal{D}D, since the normalization by F(dc)F(d_c)F(dc​) cancels.

Check with the paper's illustrative figure: effects end at 0.75 miles and the correct ring gives 0.73. With a treated ring of 1 mile, and distances spread evenly over the horizontal axis as the figure suggests, the factor is 0.75 and the formula gives about 0.55, against the 0.54 printed in the figure. If units were instead spread evenly over the area of a disc, FFF would be proportional to the squared distance and the factor would be the squared ratio of the two distances.

The equation defines the bins of the nonparametric estimator. FnF_nFn​ is the empirical distribution function of distance among the nnn units of the sample (those within dcd_cdc​), and Fn−1(q)F_n^{-1}(q)Fn−1​(q) is its qqq-th quantile. Bin jjj collects the units whose distance lies between the quantile of order (j−1)/L(j-1)/L(j−1)/L and the quantile of order j/Lj/Lj/L. With L=4L=4L=4 the bins are the four quartile groups of distance. The lowest quantile is the smallest observed distance and the highest is the largest, so the bins partition the sample; the strict inequality on the right is to be read as weak for the last bin, otherwise the most distant unit would be left out.

Quantile spacing gives every bin approximately the same number of units, n/Ln/Ln/L, so every bin mean in equation (18) has similar precision. The price is that bins are not equally wide in distance: they are narrow where units are dense and wide where they are sparse. In a two-dimensional neighborhood the number of homes grows with distance, so rings far from treatment are thinner than rings close to it, which is visible in the application figure, where the first two rings are the widest.

The bin edges are random because they depend on the sample. The inference results cited for equation (24) allow for this. Compared with equation (11), the rings are no longer chosen by the researcher: given LLL they are determined by the data, and LLL itself is chosen by a data-driven rule. As LLL grows the bins shrink to points, which is used in equations (22) and (23).

ΔY‾j\overline{\Delta Y}_jΔYj​ is the sample mean of the outcome change among the njn_jnj​ units of bin jjj. It is the fitted value of a partitioning-based least squares regression with a polynomial of degree zero in each bin: regressing the change on the full set of LLL bin indicators, without a constant, solves

min⁡b1,…,bL∑i∈D(ΔYit−∑j=1Lbj1i∈Dj)2\min_{b_1,\ldots,b_L}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}\left(\Delta Y_{it}-\sum_{j=1}^Lb_j\mathbf{1}_{i\in\mathcal{D}_j}\right)^2b1​,…,bL​min​i∈D∑​(ΔYit​−j=1∑L​bj​1i∈Dj​​)2

and the first-order condition for each coefficient sets the sum of residuals within the bin to zero, which gives b^j=ΔY‾j\hat{b}_j=\overline{\Delta Y}_jb^j​=ΔYj​. A higher-degree polynomial within bins would fit a line or a curve in each bin; the paper uses the constant because it corresponds directly to "rings" and loses nothing asymptotically.

By equation (6) and the mean independence of the error, the bin mean estimates the bin average of the sum of the two curves:

E[ΔY‾j]=E[τ(Dist)+λ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj]\mathbb{E}\left[\overline{\Delta Y}_j\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})+\lambda(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}\in\mathcal{D}_j\right]E[ΔYj​]=E[τ(Dist)+λ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj​]

(conditional on the bin edges). Its sampling variance is of order L/nL/nL/n, because the bin holds about n/Ln/Ln/L units; this is the variance side of the choice of LLL. The bin means are the building blocks of the step function in equation (19) and of the effect estimates in equation (21).

This is the fitted regression function of the binned regression, evaluated at unit iii. Exactly one indicator in the sum equals one, the one for the bin that contains the unit, so the prediction for a unit is the mean change of its own bin. Viewed as a function of distance it is a step function with LLL steps, the binscatter estimate of the conditional mean of the change given distance.

Its two sources of error are standard. The approximation error comes from replacing the conditional mean function within a bin by a constant; for a smooth function it is of the order of the bin width times the slope, so it falls as LLL rises. The sampling error of each step is of order L/n\sqrt{L/n}L/n​ and rises with LLL. The estimate converges to the conditional mean uniformly over distance when LLL grows with nnn but more slowly than nnn, so that the number of units per bin also grows, and when the conditional mean is smooth. The note states the limit as the number of bins going to infinity; the requirement that n/Ln/Ln/L also diverges is implicit.

By equation (6) the object being estimated is the sum of the effect curve and the trend curve. The step function alone therefore does not estimate the effect. Equation (20) shows that under Local Parallel Trends it estimates the effect curve shifted by a constant, and equation (21) removes the shift by subtracting the last step.

Start from the first-difference equation under Local Parallel Trends, equation (9), valid for units within dcd_cdc​. Take the expectation conditional on distance equal to ddd, with d≤dcd\leq d_cd≤dc​:

E[ΔYit∣Dist=d]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dist=d]+λ+E[Δεit∣Dist=d]\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta Y_{it}\mid\text{Dist}=d\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}=d\right]+\lambda+\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta\varepsilon_{it}\mid\text{Dist}=d\right]E[ΔYit​∣Dist=d]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dist=d]+λ+E[Δεit​∣Dist=d]

The constant passes through the expectation. The last term is zero by the mean independence of the composite error, see equation (4):

E[Δεit∣Dist=d]=E[Δuit∣Dist=d]+E[τ~i∣Dist=d]+E[λ~i∣Dist=d]=0\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta\varepsilon_{it}\mid\text{Dist}=d\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta u_{it}\mid\text{Dist}=d\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{\tau}_i\mid\text{Dist}=d\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{\lambda}_i\mid\text{Dist}=d\right]=0E[Δεit​∣Dist=d]=E[Δuit​∣Dist=d]+E[τ~i​∣Dist=d]+E[λ~i​∣Dist=d]=0

This gives the target equation. The first term on its right-hand side is simply the curve evaluated at ddd, since the curve is a deterministic function of distance:

E[ΔYit∣Dist=d]=τ(d)+λ\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta Y_{it}\mid\text{Dist}=d\right]=\tau(d)+\lambdaE[ΔYit​∣Dist=d]=τ(d)+λ

The paper writes the relation with an identity sign; it is a consequence of the model and the assumption, not a definition. The step function of equation (19) estimates the left-hand side, hence the effect curve plus an unknown constant. At any distance beyond the reach of the effect the right-hand side equals λ\lambdaλ, which is how the constant is recovered in equation (21).

The estimate of the effect on ring jjj is the mean change of that ring minus the mean change of the outermost ring, which plays the role of the control group. It is a difference-in-differences between ring jjj and ring LLL. By equations (18) and (20), under Local Parallel Trends the constant cancels in expectation:

E[τ^j]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj]−E[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈DL]\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\tau}_j\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}\in\mathcal{D}_j\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}\in\mathcal{D}_L\right]E[τ^j​]=E[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj​]−E[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈DL​]

The second term is zero when the last ring lies entirely beyond the reach of the effect. Assumption 5 guarantees that this happens once LLL is large enough, without the researcher having to know where the effect ends; this replaces Assumption 4 of equation (10). For a fixed LLL with a last ring that still contains affected units, every estimate is shifted by the mean effect of that ring.

By construction τ^L=0\hat{\tau}_L=0τ^L​=0, so the last ring carries no information and there are L−1L-1L−1 free estimates. The same numbers are obtained from a regression of the change on a constant and indicators for rings 1 to L−1L-1L−1. The ring method of equation (12) is the special case with two rings whose boundary is set by the researcher; in the application these are the rings from 0 to 0.1 miles and from 0.1 to 0.3 miles. The paper writes the last ring once with the subscript kkk and once with a lower-case lll; both mean LLL. The estimates are plotted over their intervals, they form the curve estimate of equation (22), and their standard error is equation (24).

The estimator is the step function that assigns to each unit the estimate τ^j\hat{\tau}_jτ^j​ of its bin, equation (21). The sum runs over bins jjj; the paper prints the index as iii, which is a typo, since iii is the unit and appears inside the indicator. The claim is that it converges uniformly to the effect curve when dcd_cdc​ satisfies Local Parallel Trends and Assumption 5. The argument has three steps.

Step 1, the last bin estimates the constant. Let dtd_tdt​ be the distance whose existence Assumption 5 asserts. In the population, the left edge of the last bin is the quantile qLq_LqL​ of order (L−1)/L(L-1)/L(L−1)/L of distance within the sample, defined by

F(qL)F(dc)=L−1L\frac{F(q_L)}{F(d_c)}=\frac{L-1}{L}F(dc​)F(qL​)​=LL−1​

It lies at or beyond dtd_tdt​ exactly when

L−1L≥F(dt)F(dc)⟺L≥F(dc)F(dc)−F(dt)\frac{L-1}{L}\geq\frac{F(d_t)}{F(d_c)}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L\geq\frac{F(d_c)}{F(d_c)-F(d_t)}LL−1​≥F(dc​)F(dt​)​⟺L≥F(dc​)−F(dt​)F(dc​)​

The bound is finite because part (ii) of the assumption makes the denominator positive. For all larger LLL the last bin contains only units with zero effect, and by equation (9) its mean converges to the constant as its number of units grows:

ΔY‾L→pλ\overline{\Delta Y}_L\to^p\lambdaΔYL​→pλ

Step 2, each bin estimate converges to the bin average of the curve. This is equation (23).

Step 3, bins shrink. As LLL grows, the width of the bin containing a given distance ddd goes to zero, so for a curve that is continuous at ddd

E[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj]→τ(d)\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}\in\mathcal{D}_j\right]\to\tau(d)E[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj​]→τ(d)

Combining the steps gives pointwise convergence of the step function. For a curve with slope bounded by a constant CCC the approximation error is bounded by CCC times the largest bin width at every distance at once, which, together with a uniform bound on the sampling error of the bin means, gives the uniform statement

sup⁡d≤dc∣τ^(d)−τ(d)∣→p0\sup_{d\leq d_c}\left|\hat{\tau}(d)-\tau(d)\right|\to^p0d≤dc​sup​∣τ^(d)−τ(d)∣→p0

The paper takes this last part from Cattaneo, Farrell and Feng. Two conditions are left unstated in the paper and in the note. First, LLL must grow more slowly than nnn, so that the number of units per bin, about n/Ln/Ln/L, also diverges; otherwise the bin means in steps 1 and 2 do not converge. Second, uniform convergence requires a continuous curve. A curve with a jump, which Assumption 4 permits and which the simulation curves τ1\tau_1τ1​ and τ4\tau_4τ4​ of equation (26) have, is recovered at every continuity point but not uniformly near the jump. The summation index jjj and the last ring DL\mathcal{D}_LDL​ in the note are the correct readings of the paper.

Start from the definition in equation (21) and substitute equation (9) into each bin mean of equation (18). For any bin jjj:

ΔY‾j=1nj∑i∈Djτ(Disti)+λ+1nj∑i∈DjΔεit\overline{\Delta Y}_j=\frac{1}{n_j}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_j}\tau(\text{Dist}_i)+\lambda+\frac{1}{n_j}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_j}\Delta\varepsilon_{it}ΔYj​=nj​1​i∈Dj​∑​τ(Disti​)+λ+nj​1​i∈Dj​∑​Δεit​

Local Parallel Trends is what makes the middle term the same constant in every bin. Hold LLL fixed and let nnn grow, so that njn_jnj​ grows as well. By the law of large numbers within the bin, with random sampling and mean independence of the error from distance, the first average converges to the bin mean of the curve and the last average converges to zero:

ΔY‾j→pE[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj]+λ\overline{\Delta Y}_j\to^p\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}\in\mathcal{D}_j\right]+\lambdaΔYj​→pE[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj​]+λ

The estimated bin edges converge to the population quantiles, so the conditioning set can be taken as the population bin. Apply the same result to the last bin. By step 1 of equation (22), for LLL large enough the last bin lies beyond the reach of the effect, so its limit is the constant alone:

ΔY‾L→pE[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈DL]+λ=λ\overline{\Delta Y}_L\to^p\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}\in\mathcal{D}_L\right]+\lambda=\lambdaΔYL​→pE[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈DL​]+λ=λ

Subtract, using the fact that the difference of two sequences that converge in probability converges to the difference of the limits:

τ^j=ΔY‾j−ΔY‾L→pE[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj]+λ−λ=E[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj]\hat{\tau}_j=\overline{\Delta Y}_j-\overline{\Delta Y}_L\to^p\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}\in\mathcal{D}_j\right]+\lambda-\lambda=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(\text{Dist})\mid\text{Dist}\in\mathcal{D}_j\right]τ^j​=ΔYj​−ΔYL​→pE[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj​]+λ−λ=E[τ(Dist)∣Dist∈Dj​]

Each estimate therefore converges to the average treatment effect of its own ring. This is the finite-LLL interpretation used in the application. If the last bin still contained affected units, the limit would instead be the bin average minus the average effect in the last bin, and all estimates would be shifted by the same amount.

The estimate for ring jjj, with j<Lj<Lj<L, is a difference of two bin means, equation (21). The variance of a difference is

Var⁡(τ^j)=Var⁡(ΔY‾j)+Var⁡(ΔY‾L)−2Cov⁡(ΔY‾j,ΔY‾L)\operatorname{Var}\left(\hat{\tau}_j\right)=\operatorname{Var}\left(\overline{\Delta Y}_j\right)+\operatorname{Var}\left(\overline{\Delta Y}_L\right)-2\operatorname{Cov}\left(\overline{\Delta Y}_j,\overline{\Delta Y}_L\right)Var(τ^j​)=Var(ΔYj​)+Var(ΔYL​)−2Cov(ΔYj​,ΔYL​)

The two means are computed from disjoint sets of units. Under random sampling (Assumption 1) the units are independent, so conditional on the assignment of units to bins the covariance is zero:

Cov⁡(ΔY‾j,ΔY‾L)=1njnL∑i∈Dj∑i′∈DLCov⁡(ΔYit,ΔYi′t)=0\operatorname{Cov}\left(\overline{\Delta Y}_j,\overline{\Delta Y}_L\right)=\frac{1}{n_jn_L}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_j}\sum_{i'\in\mathcal{D}_L}\operatorname{Cov}\left(\Delta Y_{it},\Delta Y_{i't}\right)=0Cov(ΔYj​,ΔYL​)=nj​nL​1​i∈Dj​∑​i′∈DL​∑​Cov(ΔYit​,ΔYi′t​)=0

Write σj\sigma_jσj​ for the standard error of the mean of bin jjj and σL\sigma_LσL​ for that of the last bin, so that the two variances are estimated by their squares. Then

se⁡(τ^j)=σj2+σL2\operatorname{se}\left(\hat{\tau}_j\right)=\sqrt{\sigma_j^2+\sigma_L^2}se(τ^j​)=σj2​+σL2​​

which is the target. With a heteroskedasticity-robust variance each term is approximately the within-bin variance of the change divided by the number of units in the bin, so with equal-sized bins and equal variances the standard error is 2\sqrt{2}2​ times that of a single bin mean. The same σL\sigma_LσL​ enters every estimate, so the estimates for different rings are positively correlated through the common control ring; the formula is pointwise and says nothing about joint statements over rings.

Qualifications. The formula applies to j<Lj<Lj<L; for j=Lj=Lj=L the estimate is identically zero and has no sampling error. Zero covariance relies on independence across units. The paper argues that no spatial correction is needed because the error is uncorrelated with distance, but errors that are correlated between neighbouring homes would make both the bin variances and the covariance differ from the expressions above, and being uncorrelated with distance does not exclude that. Finally, the bin edges are estimated quantiles; the standard errors of Cattaneo, Crump, Farrell and Feng account for this, and the independence argument is then an approximation that holds in large samples.

This is the data-generating process of the Monte Carlo exercise, taken from Diamond and McQuade (2019). pitp_{it}pit​ is the simulated price of unit iii in period ttt. The intercept is one. The terms with the coordinates Lati\text{Lat}_iLati​ and Loni\text{Lon}_iLoni​ give a time-invariant price gradient over space, a tilted plane. λ\lambdaλ multiplies the period-1 indicator and is a trend common to all units, so Local Parallel Trends, equation (7), holds exactly at every distance. The curve τ(Disti)\tau(\text{Dist}_i)τ(Disti​) is switched on in period 1 and is one of the four curves of equation (26). The error is independent of distance.

The process is a special case of equation (3). The unit effect is the sum of the intercept and the spatial plane, there is no idiosyncratic heterogeneity in effects or trends, and first differencing removes the plane:

μi=1+βLatLati+βLonLoni,Δpit=τ(Disti)+λ+Δεit\mu_i=1+\beta_{\text{Lat}}\text{Lat}_i+\beta_{\text{Lon}}\text{Lon}_i,\qquad\Delta p_{it}=\tau(\text{Dist}_i)+\lambda+\Delta\varepsilon_{it}μi​=1+βLat​Lati​+βLon​Loni​,Δpit​=τ(Disti​)+λ+Δεit​

which is equation (9). The spatial gradient therefore plays no role for estimators based on differences; it matters only for cross-sectional methods. The coefficients βLat\beta_{\text{Lat}}βLat​, βLon\beta_{\text{Lon}}βLon​ and the trend λ\lambdaλ are drawn once per simulation, the error for every unit and period. The paper does not say whether the second argument of each normal distribution is a variance or a standard deviation. Units are placed on the unit disc with treatment at its centre, so distances range from zero to one, which matches the outer ring limit of one in the ring specifications. The design is favourable to both methods in one respect: the trend assumption is true, so differences in performance come only from how each method approximates the curve.

These are the four treatment effect curves of the simulations, each multiplied by an indicator that sets the effect to zero beyond a cutoff. The notation with an asterisk is ordinary multiplication.

τ1\tau_1τ1​ is a step: 0.15 up to distance 0.4 and zero beyond, the shape for which one ring with the right cutoff is exactly correct. τ2\tau_2τ2​ is the decreasing convex curve of Diamond and McQuade (2019); it equals 0.32 at distance zero, 0.08 at 0.4, 0.02 at 0.6, and reaches zero continuously at 0.8. τ4\tau_4τ4​ is the same parabola cut off at 0.25, where it jumps from about 0.151 to zero, so only the closest units are affected. τ3\tau_3τ3​ is a concave parabola that factors as

−0.15+1.2875 d−1.375 d2=−1.375(d−322)(d−0.8)-0.15+1.2875\,d-1.375\,d^2=-1.375\left(d-\tfrac{3}{22}\right)\left(d-0.8\right)−0.15+1.2875d−1.375d2=−1.375(d−223​)(d−0.8)

so it equals −0.15-0.15−0.15 at distance zero, crosses zero at 3/22≈0.1363/22\approx0.1363/22≈0.136, peaks at about 0.151 near d=0.47d=0.47d=0.47 and returns to zero continuously at 0.8.

Two statements in the note about τ3\tau_3τ3​, both taken from the paper's text, do not match the printed formula. The curve turns positive at about 0.14, not around 0.3. And its average over affected units is not near zero: it is about 0.07 if distances are uniform on the interval from 0 to 0.8, and about 0.10 if units are uniform over the area of the disc, compared with a peak of 0.15. The curve is negative only on a short interval that holds few units.

The printed ring boundaries (inner rings ending at 0.6) do not coincide with the reach of any of the curves, which is 0.4, 0.8, 0.8 and 0.25. With those rings Assumption 4 of equation (10) fails in every design: the treated ring is too wide for τ1\tau_1τ1​ and τ4\tau_4τ4​, where equation (16) applies, and too narrow for τ2\tau_2τ2​ and τ3\tau_3τ3​. This contradicts the paper's statement, repeated in the note, that the ring specifications satisfy the correct maximum treatment distance. The prediction error used to compare the estimators is equation (27).

υi\upsilon_iυi​ is the prediction error of an estimated curve at the location of unit iii: the estimated effect at that unit's distance minus the true effect from equation (26). For a ring estimator the estimated curve is a step function with one value per ring, and zero in the control ring; for the nonparametric estimator it is the step function of equation (22). The error is computed for every unit in every simulated sample and summarized in three ways:

E^(υi2)=1N+∑i: τ(Disti)>0υi2,E^(∣υi∣)=1N+∑i: τ(Disti)>0∣υi∣\hat{E}\left(\upsilon_i^2\right)=\frac{1}{N_{+}}\sum_{i:\,\tau(\text{Dist}_i)>0}\upsilon_i^2,\qquad\hat{E}\left(|\upsilon_i|\right)=\frac{1}{N_{+}}\sum_{i:\,\tau(\text{Dist}_i)>0}|\upsilon_i|E^(υi2​)=N+​1​i:τ(Disti​)>0∑​υi2​,E^(∣υi​∣)=N+​1​i:τ(Disti​)>0∑​∣υi​∣

where N+N_{+}N+​ is the number of observations with a positive true effect, pooled over the 2000 simulations, together with the mean error at a distance of 0.4. The mean squared error combines the squared approximation bias of the estimator at each distance with its sampling variance, so it rewards an estimator that gets the shape of the curve right and penalizes one that is noisy. The absolute error is less sensitive to large misses.

Each summary is reported as a ratio to the value for the nonparametric estimator. A ratio above one means that the ring method is worse. The pattern over sample sizes follows from the bias and variance split: the ring estimators have a bias that does not fall with nnn when the curve is not flat, while the nonparametric estimator has both bias and variance falling with nnn, so the ratios rise with nnn for τ2\tau_2τ2​, τ3\tau_3τ3​ and τ4\tau_4τ4​. Two details deserve care. Averaging only over units with a positive effect leaves out the negative part of τ3\tau_3τ3​ and the errors made on unaffected units. And the true value of τ1\tau_1τ1​ at a distance of exactly 0.4 is zero, because its indicator uses a strict inequality.
